concerns: Key inference (TFF shear → loss of membrane-protected capture signal independent of particle counts) is not directly supported by cited evidence; MISEV2023 supports orthogonal analytics but does not provide empirical TFF causality.
Driedonks et al. is appropriately cited as limiting/translational biodistribution evidence, but it does not demonstrate TFF-induced membrane damage and should not be over-interpreted as such.
Proposal relies on qualitative recovery metrics without predefined numeric acceptance criteria; program-level decisions will require quantitative gates and robustness statistics.

Assay interference (buffer effects, capture reagent compatibility) and source-cell variability are acknowledged but represent plausible competing explanations that must be excluded by validated spike-in controls and orthogonal assays prior to interpreting results.

Preserving an orthogonal analytic signature is treated as a necessary precondition for potency linkage, but no evidentiary link to improved in vivo delivery or potency is provided; downstream bridging experiments are required and may be confounded by route/species biodistribution issues.
conclusion: Not supported as written. The proposal is plausible and cites appropriate guidance about analytic orthogonality (MISEV2023) and a cautionary non-human-primate biodistribution study, but there is no direct published evidence that high-TMP/high-flux TFF conditions cause loss of membrane-protected capture signals (while leaving bulk particle counts unchanged) or that the specific staged low-shear envelope described will preserve those signatures across lots. The claim is therefore an inference-level hypothesis that requires the proposed pilot experiments and validated spike-in controls before it can be accepted as supported.
evidence_gap: No direct experimental literature demonstrating that TFF operating envelope (high-TMP/high-flux versus staged low-shear) causes or prevents loss of an orthogonal intact‑EV capture/protection signature (co-localized capture-positive particle peaks and detergent/protease sensitivity). Also missing are published, validated spike-in tracer methods and buffer/capture-compatibility data that would exclude assay interference as the cause of signature loss. Finally, there is no published evidence that preservation of this analytic signature improves in vivo detectability or potency (species/route-dependent delivery barriers remain unaddressed).
